task_1.title: Restore tuple-style representation for groupby results
task_1.description: Jinja 2.9.5 restores the pre-2.9 string and repr behavior of values produced by the `groupby` filter. The grouped result still exposes the same two-part structure, but it should present itself like a plain tuple rather than a namedtuple so downstream tooling that depends on tuple-style output remains compatible.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that values returned by the `groupby` filter are represented to users and downstream consumers like plain tuples again, so upgrades from versions before 2.9 do not break integrations that rely on tuple-style output.

expectation.grounded: The `groupby` filter should continue returning `_GroupTuple` items with `grouper` and `list` fields, but the observable `repr()` and `str()` of each result item must match regular tuple formatting instead of the namedtuple-style representation introduced in 2.9.x. This restores the previous externally visible behavior for consumers that print, log, serialize, or parse these values.
expectation.conceptual: Grouped values from `groupby` should still behave as two-part group records, while their displayed form should look the same as it did before the 2.9 series. Users and integrations should see tuple-style output rather than an implementation-specific namedtuple display.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the grouping contract of `groupby`: each result item must remain a two-element grouped record with attribute access for the group key and grouped items. Only the externally visible string and repr formatting should revert to tuple-style output, avoiding exposure of the internal custom type name in normal display.
constraints.conceptual: The fix should preserve existing grouping behavior and data shape while narrowing the change to how grouped results are presented externally. Upgrading should improve compatibility without changing how callers iterate over or access grouped data.

behavior: Calling `groupby` still yields grouped records containing the group key and the list of matching items.
Each grouped record continues to support the existing two-field access pattern for the key and grouped values.
The string form of a grouped record is rendered as a plain tuple representation instead of a namedtuple-style representation.
The repr form of a grouped record is rendered as a plain tuple representation instead of a namedtuple-style representation.
The internal custom type used by `groupby` should not be exposed through normal stringification of grouped records.
acceptance_criteria: When a template or integration uses the `groupby` filter, each returned group item should remain a two-part record containing the grouping key and the grouped items.
When code accesses the grouped result by its existing field names, it should continue to work after the upgrade.
When a grouped record is converted to a string, it should appear in plain tuple form rather than including a namedtuple type-style display.
When a grouped record is inspected with `repr()`, it should appear in plain tuple form rather than including a namedtuple type-style display.
When existing downstream tooling depends on tuple-like textual output from `groupby`, upgrading to 2.9.5 should restore compatibility with that expectation.

task_2.title: Restore compatibility for custom Context.resolve overrides
task_2.description: Version 2.9.5 restores backward-compatible variable resolution for applications that provide custom Jinja2 Context subclasses overriding the legacy resolve() method. The update ensures those custom contexts continue to influence template variable lookup and missing-value handling without requiring an additional resolve_or_missing() override, while preserving existing behavior for standard contexts.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.9.5 preserves expected template variable lookup for custom Jinja2 context classes that override the legacy resolve() method, so existing integrations do not regress when resolving provided values, inherited context values, or missing names.

expectation.grounded: If an application defines a jinja2.runtime.Context subclass that overrides Context.resolve() but does not override Context.resolve_or_missing(), Jinja2 should continue to honor that custom resolve() logic during runtime lookup. In that compatibility case, Context.resolve_or_missing() should reflect values returned by the custom resolve(), convert Undefined results into the internal missing sentinel, and still allow standard parent and local context lookup behavior to remain observable through Context.resolve(). For contexts that do not customize resolution, the default Context.resolve() and Context.resolve_or_missing() behavior should remain unchanged.
expectation.conceptual: Custom context classes that rely on the older variable-resolution hook should keep working after the upgrade. Template rendering should still see custom-resolved values, ordinary context values should still be found normally, and missing names should still be treated as missing rather than as successful resolutions.

constraints.grounded: Do not require existing custom Context subclasses to add a resolve_or_missing() override in order to preserve pre-2.9.5 behavior. Do not change the observable contract of Context.resolve() returning an Undefined for unresolved names and Context.resolve_or_missing() returning a missing sentinel for unresolved names. Do not regress default lookup order through context vars and parent data for non-custom contexts.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must preserve backward compatibility for older custom context integrations, keep missing-value semantics stable, and avoid changing normal variable lookup behavior for users who are not customizing context resolution.

behavior: A custom Context subclass that overrides resolve() is treated as using legacy custom resolution semantics even if it leaves resolve_or_missing() unchanged.
Under that legacy compatibility path, resolve() continues to return custom values when the override supplies them.
Under that legacy compatibility path, resolve_or_missing() derives its result from the custom resolve() behavior and reports unresolved names as missing rather than as Undefined objects.

Default Context instances and subclasses that do not customize resolution continue to resolve from local context variables first, then parent context values, and report absent names as missing or Undefined according to the public API used.
acceptance_criteria: When an application uses a custom Context subclass that overrides resolve() to supply a value for a name, rendering logic that depends on context resolution should observe that supplied value after upgrading to 2.9.5.
When that same custom Context subclass is asked for a name that exists in the normal context data, it should still resolve that name successfully.

When that same custom Context subclass is asked for a name that is not available from either custom logic or context data, resolve_or_missing() should report it as missing and resolve() should expose it as Undefined.
When an application uses the default Context behavior without custom resolution overrides, variable lookup and missing-name handling should remain unchanged from prior behavior.

task_3.title: Fix recursive for-else template rendering regression
task_3.description: Jinja 2.9.5 fixes a regression in recursive for-loops that include an else clause. In 2.9.4, these templates could fail to compile on Python 2.x or render fallback output incorrectly on Python 3; the update restores correct compilation and output behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that recursive template for-loops with an else clause compile and render correctly, so empty iterables produce the fallback output instead of causing syntax failures or incorrect rendered results.

expectation.grounded: Templates created through public Jinja APIs such as `jinja2.Template` or `Environment.from_string` that contain a recursive `{% for %}` loop with an `{% else %}` branch should compile successfully and render the `else` branch into the final output when the iterable is empty. The regression seen in 2.9.4 should no longer produce a `SyntaxError` during compilation on Python 2.x, and the recursive loop's `else` output should be emitted through the same rendered output stream as the loop body.
expectation.conceptual: Recursive loop templates should handle `else` the same way users expect from normal loop constructs: if there are no items, the fallback content renders normally, and the template remains valid to compile and render across supported runtimes.

constraints.grounded: The fix must preserve existing behavior for non-empty recursive loops and must not change standard loop semantics outside the broken recursive `for` plus `else` case. The `else` branch must not be dropped, isolated, or rendered inconsistently relative to the rest of the template output.
constraints.conceptual: Correct the broken fallback behavior without changing output for loop scenarios that already work.

behavior: Compiling a template that contains a recursive `for` loop with an `else` clause no longer generates invalid syntax on Python 2.x.
Rendering a recursive `for` loop with an empty iterable emits the `else` branch output as part of the template result.
The fallback output from the `else` branch is written into the same final rendered result as the recursive loop body, preventing missing or misdirected content.
acceptance_criteria: When a template uses a recursive `for` loop with an `else` clause and the iterable is empty, rendering it should return the fallback content from `else` in the template output.
When such a template is compiled from source through the public template creation APIs, it should not fail with a syntax-related compilation error.
When the iterable is non-empty, the recursive loop should continue to render its body normally with no regression in output behavior.

task_4.title: Fix async template inheritance for extends
task_4.description: Jinja 2.9.5 fixes a runtime compilation issue that prevented templates using `{% extends %}` from working in async environments. Inherited templates should now load and render correctly in async mode while preserving existing synchronous inheritance behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates using `{% extends %}` can be loaded, compiled, and rendered in async-enabled environments without failing because of async-incompatible inheritance handling.

expectation.grounded: In an async-enabled Jinja environment, a template that uses the `{% extends %}` tag must compile and render inherited output successfully instead of failing with a syntax-level async/yield incompatibility during template loading or compilation. Template inheritance must remain supported for parent template rendering in async execution.
expectation.conceptual: Template inheritance should work in async mode the same way users expect it to work in normal mode: extending a parent template should succeed and produce inherited output without async-specific compilation failures.

constraints.grounded: The change must address async handling of parent template rendering for `{% extends %}` without altering established inheritance behavior in synchronous environments or changing the resulting inherited output sequence.
constraints.conceptual: The fix should remove the async-mode failure while preserving existing inheritance behavior and rendered results for non-async usage.

behavior: Templates containing `{% extends %}` are supported in async-enabled Jinja environments.
Loading or compiling an inherited template in async mode no longer fails with a syntax error caused by async-incompatible parent template iteration.
Rendering an inherited template in async mode produces parent-template output through async-compatible inheritance handling.
Synchronous template inheritance behavior remains unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: When an async-enabled Jinja environment loads or compiles a template that uses `{% extends %}`, it should succeed without raising a syntax-level async/yield incompatibility error.
When that inherited template is rendered in async mode, it should include parent-template output according to normal Jinja inheritance semantics.
When template inheritance is used in a synchronous environment, the rendered behavior and output should remain consistent with prior releases.

task_5.title: Reduce Unicode Identifier Matching Memory Use
task_5.description: Jinja 2.9.5 reduces runtime memory used for Unicode identifier matching on Python 3 by shipping only the identifier character data the lexer actually needs and discarding the temporary lookup module after the lexer regex is built. Identifier recognition behavior is intended to remain the same for supported Unicode names, while ASCII-only fallback behavior remains available on runtimes without Unicode identifier support.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to Jinja 2.9.5 reduces the memory footprint of Unicode identifier handling on Python 3 without changing which template identifiers are recognized or regressing ASCII-only fallback behavior on runtimes that do not support Unicode identifiers.

expectation.grounded: On runtimes where `jinja2.lexer` can compile Unicode identifiers, `name_re` should continue to be derived from `jinja2._stringdefs.xid_start` and `jinja2._stringdefs.xid_continue`, but the shipped `_stringdefs` data should be limited to those XID sets instead of full Unicode category dumps. After building the regex, the temporary `jinja2._stringdefs` module should no longer remain loaded solely for identifier matching. On runtimes where compiling a Unicode identifier fails, the lexer should still fall back to the existing ASCII identifier pattern.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should lower memory retained for identifier parsing, especially on Python 3, while preserving the same observable identifier acceptance rules for valid Unicode names and keeping the existing ASCII-only fallback on interpreters that cannot use Unicode identifiers.

constraints.grounded: Do not broaden or narrow the lexer's accepted identifier set relative to the XID-based matching already used for Unicode-capable runtimes. Do not remove the ASCII fallback path for runtimes that raise `SyntaxError` when compiling a Unicode identifier. The change must remain a memory optimization rather than a functional parser rewrite.
constraints.conceptual: Template authors should not need to rename identifiers or change templates because of this upgrade. The change must act as a transparent optimization and preserve compatibility across both Unicode-capable and ASCII-only interpreter behavior.

behavior: On Python 3, the packaged Unicode lookup data used for identifier matching is reduced to the `xid_start` and `xid_continue` sets actually consumed by the lexer.
When Unicode identifiers are supported by the interpreter, the lexer still compiles its identifier regex from those XID character sets and continues recognizing valid Unicode identifiers as names.
After the Unicode identifier regex is constructed, the temporary `_stringdefs` module is removed from retained module state so it does not continue occupying memory unnecessarily.
If the interpreter cannot compile a Unicode identifier, lexer setup continues to use the ASCII identifier regex instead of relying on Unicode tables.
acceptance_criteria: When Jinja initializes on a Python 3 runtime that supports Unicode identifiers, it should retain less memory for identifier matching data than version 2.9.4 while continuing to parse the same valid Unicode identifiers.
When a template contains identifiers composed of characters allowed by Jinja's Unicode identifier rules, the lexer should continue to recognize them as names on Unicode-capable runtimes.
When Jinja runs on a runtime that rejects Unicode identifiers at compile time, lexer initialization should still succeed by using the ASCII identifier pattern.
When applications import and use the lexer repeatedly, the upgrade should not leave the Unicode lookup module resident solely because the identifier regex was created.

task_6.title: Fix async macro autoescaping in Jinja2 2.9.5
task_6.description: Jinja2 2.9.5 fixes macro rendering in async mode when autoescaping is enabled. Macro calls made during asynchronous template rendering should now resolve to their rendered content with normal autoescape behavior instead of surfacing coroutine output or leaving async macro execution unfinished.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that template macros render correctly during asynchronous execution when autoescaping is enabled, so users receive the macro's rendered output with normal escaping behavior instead of coroutine-like output or incomplete async execution.

expectation.grounded: When templates are created with async execution enabled and rendered through asynchronous rendering APIs, macro calls must execute through an async-aware macro invocation path. If autoescaping is active, the macro result must be processed with the same escaping/markup semantics as synchronous macro calls after the async result is resolved. Macro evaluation must yield rendered template content rather than exposing a coroutine representation, and async macro execution must complete without unawaited-coroutine warnings caused by macro invocation.
expectation.conceptual: In asynchronous template rendering, calling a macro should behave the same as normal rendering from the user's perspective: the macro should finish executing, produce its rendered value, and honor autoescaping consistently.

constraints.grounded: This fix must preserve existing macro behavior for non-async environments and for the synchronous invocation path. The change must not alter the public way macros are called from templates, and autoescape handling must remain tied to whether autoescaping is enabled for the current rendering context.
constraints.conceptual: The update should only correct broken async macro behavior and should not change how macros work in regular rendering or when escaping settings are unchanged.

behavior: Macro calls made during asynchronous template rendering now follow a dedicated async invocation path instead of directly returning the raw async function result.
When async macro execution is used, the macro result is resolved before autoescape processing is applied.
With autoescaping enabled, async macro output is returned as rendered, escaped content rather than a coroutine object's textual representation.
In non-async environments, macro invocation continues to use the existing synchronous behavior.
acceptance_criteria: When a template enables asynchronous rendering and autoescaping, calling a macro during async rendering should produce the macro's rendered output rather than a coroutine representation.
When a macro returns content during asynchronous rendering with autoescaping enabled, the returned content should reflect normal autoescape behavior.
When the same macro is rendered in a non-async environment, its behavior should remain unchanged from prior synchronous behavior.
When asynchronous rendering invokes macros, macro execution should complete as part of rendering rather than leaving an unawaited coroutine observable to the user.
